lessons.subject: french
lessons.lesson_title: Keep Tu With Vas in Questions
lessons.previous_learning: Five of your six written sentences were correct. In your question, tu needed vas instead of va. Your oral round was not submitted.
lessons.course_context: Day 27 follows the September 30 submitted work. Repair the named gap before moving to the next unit.
learning_objectives: Match tu with vas every time
Keep the action verb in its basic form
Make a question and a negative sentence
lessons.why_it_matters: Getting the small middle word right makes the whole sentence work.

vocabulary.definition: the person doing the action
the French verb meaning to go
the basic action word before changing it
a pattern meaning going to do something

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 10:30 to 11:00, 30 minutes. Stop and move on at 11:00.
To say going to do something, use a subject, its form of aller, and the basic action word. The first verb changes for the person; the second stays in its basic form.
je vais; tu vas; il or elle va; nous allons; vous allez; ils or elles vont. Tu means you for one familiar person.
MODEL: Tu vas dessiner. You are going to draw. Add Est-ce que at the start to ask a question: Est-ce que tu vas dessiner ? Tu still needs vas. The question starter does not change the verb.
For a negative, put ne and pas around the form of aller: Elle ne va pas dessiner. She is not going to draw. Before a vowel, ne becomes n': Nous n'allons pas dessiner.
Today's action words: jouer = play; regarder = watch; manger = eat; lire = read; partir = leave; étudier = study.
Say who first, then choose the matching form, then add the basic action word. Read your entire sentence to check the match.

worked_examples.title: Question keeps the same verb
worked_examples.problem: Turn Tu vas dessiner into a question.
worked_examples.explanation: Tu keeps vas. Dessiner stays in its basic form.

worked_examples.title: Negative sentence
worked_examples.problem: She is not going to draw.
worked_examples.explanation: Ne and pas surround va, not dessiner.

independent_practice.prompt: F1. Translate: You are going to eat. Use tu.
F2. Turn Tu vas jouer into an Est-ce que question.
F3. Translate: She is going to read.
F4. Make negative: Nous allons regarder le match.
independent_practice.answer: Nous n'allons pas regarder le match.

independent_practice.prompt: F5. Translate: They are not going to leave. Use ils.
F6. Turn Tu vas étudier into an Est-ce que question.

exit_ticket.prompt: FE1. Without the chart, say three new sentences: You are going to watch (tu); Are you going to read (tu); We are not going to play. Have your parent record correct or retry for each.
exit_ticket.answer: Tu vas regarder. Est-ce que tu vas lire ? Nous n'allons pas jouer. Written 6/6 and oral 3/3 after repair; do not invent oral results.

lessons.voice_prompt: Keep this short. Oral cues use different action words from written questions. Correct tu/vas first. Record oral evidence only if actually observed. Teach each word before using it. Show the lesson picture first, then draw one different example on the whiteboard. Ask one question at a time. Keep assigned answers protected. At the time limit, mark unfinished work for review and move to the next subject. Today is the revised 10:30 AM to 3:30 PM day. lessons.subject: science
lessons.lesson_title: Make Light Turn at Both Mirrors
lessons.previous_learning: You drew two mirrors, arrows, and angle labels. The second ray kept travelling straight past Mirror 2. Today you will make a real turn and draw each normal at a square corner to its mirror.
lessons.course_context: Day 27 follows the September 30 submitted work. Repair the named gap before moving to the next unit.
learning_objectives: Draw a normal at a right angle to each mirror
Measure both angles from the normal
Make a valid turn at both mirrors
lessons.why_it_matters: A clear drawing lets you test whether light could really reach the target.

vocabulary.definition: a line showing the direction light travels
light bouncing from a surface
a helper line at a square corner to the mirror
travelling toward the mirror
travelling away from the mirror
how wide a turn opens
the numbers used to measure angles
the spot where the ray touches the mirror
meeting at a square corner

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 11:00 to 11:45, 45 minutes. Stop and move on at 11:45.
Draw a mirror as a straight line. At the hit point, draw a dashed helper line at a right angle to it. This helper is called the normal. Perpendicular means the two lines make a square corner.
The incoming ray moves toward the hit point. The outgoing ray moves away from it. Put arrows on both so the direction is clear.
Measure each angle from the normal, not from the mirror surface. If the incoming ray makes 45 degrees with the normal, the outgoing ray makes 45 degrees on the other side. The dashed line sits between them.
Look at the two-mirror model. The ray goes right to Mirror 1, turns up to Mirror 2, then turns right to the target. Both tilted mirrors have their own tilted normal. There is a new turn at each mirror.
A ray that passes straight through the hit point has not made the required bounce. Writing equal angle numbers does not fix a path that does not match the picture.
Turning Mirror 1 also turns its normal. The reflected direction changes, so the ray may miss Mirror 2. After any change, check the whole path again.
A protractor is a tool for measuring angles. Ask for one if available; without one, use the supplied 45-degree model and the right-angle square as guides. Do not guess a precise measurement from a rough sketch.

worked_examples.title: A single bounce
worked_examples.problem: A ray meets a mirror at 45 degrees to its normal.
worked_examples.solution: The outgoing ray is on the other side of the normal at 45 degrees.
worked_examples.explanation: Angles are measured from the dashed normal.

worked_examples.title: Two separate bounces
worked_examples.problem: A ray travels right to the first tilted mirror, then up to the second.
worked_examples.solution: The second mirror sends the ray right toward the target in this model.
worked_examples.explanation: At each mirror, draw a new normal and reflect about it.

independent_practice.prompt: S1. Redraw the single-mirror model. Label the mirror, hit point, normal, incoming ray, and outgoing ray. Mark the right angle between mirror and normal.
independent_practice.answer: All labels correct; normal perpendicular; arrows toward and away; equal angles about normal.

independent_practice.prompt: S2. Create a two-mirror route with a source on the left and a target above the source. Use the model as a guide but turn or move the whole route. Draw a new normal at each hit point and make the ray change direction at both mirrors. Mark equal incoming and outgoing angles measured from each normal.
independent_practice.answer: Two physically consistent reflections, arrows, two perpendicular normals, two hit points, angles measured from normals. No straight-through second hit.

independent_practice.prompt: S3. Write three sentences explaining how turning Mirror 1 could make the ray miss Mirror 2. Name the normal in your explanation.
independent_practice.answer: Mirror 1 and normal turn; reflected direction changes; ray may no longer reach mirror 2.

exit_ticket.prompt: SE1. If the incoming ray makes 30 degrees with the normal, what angle should the outgoing ray make with the normal? Where is the outgoing ray compared with the incoming ray?
exit_ticket.answer: 30 degrees on the other side of the normal, on the same side of the mirror surface.

exit_ticket.prompt: SE2. Point to the second mirror in your drawing. Explain how your arrows prove there is a second bounce.
exit_ticket.answer: Incoming arrow points toward hit point; outgoing points away in a reflected direction, not straight through.

lessons.voice_prompt: Start with one mirror, one hit point, one right-angle normal. Use a different ray path on the whiteboard. Do not accept equal written angle labels as proof. Inspect the second bounce explicitly. Teach each word before using it. Show the lesson picture first, then draw one different example on the whiteboard. Ask one question at a time. Keep assigned answers protected. At the time limit, mark unfinished work for review and move to the next subject. Today is the revised 10:30 AM to 3:30 PM day. Math and writing are deferred; do not assign them or use spare time for them. Stop this block at 11:45.
lessons.teacher_notes: September 30 science 11/20 = 55%. Labels exist, but normals are not reliably perpendicular and second reflection is drawn straight through. Reward diagrams consistent with the law, not just copied numbers. Revised October 1 schedule. Math and writing deferred at parent request; not missing work and not zero grades.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: You correctly named the Italian Peninsula and explained rivers, farmland, and hills. Your final geography answer needed to explain why a useful location alone does not guarantee success.
lessons.course_context: Day 27 follows the September 30 submitted work. Repair the named gap before moving to the next unit.
learning_objectives: Connect a Roman feature to a human action
Explain why an advantage does not guarantee success
lessons.why_it_matters: History gets clearer when you explain how people used a place.

vocabulary.definition: the land and water around a place
land with water around three sides
something that can help
buying, selling, or exchanging goods
make sure something will happen

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 11:55 to 12:45, 50 minutes. Stop and move on at 12:45.
VIDEO FIRST: Open Ancient Rome 101 by National Geographic: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/ancient-rome-101/ Watch once, then replay the opening about the Tiber River. Spend up to 10 minutes watching and pausing. The video previews later Roman history; today you only need to explain a place, what people did there, and a possible result. A civilization is a large community with shared ways of living, such as government, buildings, and trade.
BEFORE WATCHING: Point to the river in the lesson picture. Predict one way people could use a river. AFTER WATCHING: Say one detail you noticed and one question. Return to the river, farmland, and hills model for the written work.
Rome developed on the Italian Peninsula beside the Tiber River. The nearby farmland could grow food. Hills could help people defend the city. River routes could help boats carry goods.
These were advantages: helpful possibilities. People still had to farm the land, use the river, organize trade, and build defenses.
Use three steps: FEATURE, PEOPLE'S ACTION, POSSIBLE RESULT. Feature means the part of the place you are discussing. For example: farmland; farmers plant and harvest crops; more people can be fed.
A useful location does not guarantee success. A city can have good farmland but still struggle if people cannot grow or share enough food. Choices, cooperation, and conflict also affect what happens.
Do not say Rome was unsuccessful just because geography was not the only cause. Say geography helped, but people's actions also mattered.
Today we finish this explanation before starting the Roman Republic.

worked_examples.title: An advantage needs action
worked_examples.problem: A city has farmland nearby. Why might that help?
worked_examples.solution: Farmers can grow food there, which can feed more people.
worked_examples.explanation: Land alone does not grow, harvest, or distribute food without people doing the work.

worked_examples.title: An opportunity is not a guarantee
worked_examples.problem: Imagine a town beside a useful road. Does the road alone guarantee trade?
worked_examples.solution: No. People must carry goods on the road and arrange exchanges.
worked_examples.explanation: The feature creates an opportunity. People must use it. This is a general model, not a new fact about Rome.

independent_practice.prompt: H1. Write a three-step explanation for the Tiber River: feature, people's action, possible result.
independent_practice.answer: Tiber River; people use boats for carrying goods; trade becomes easier.

independent_practice.prompt: H2. Write a three-step explanation for farmland: feature, people's action, possible result.
independent_practice.answer: Farmland; farmers grow crops; growing population can be fed.

independent_practice.prompt: H3. Repair this sentence: Geography alone made Rome successful. Write two sentences naming an advantage and a human action.
independent_practice.answer: Geography gave Rome advantages such as river routes, but people had to use them for transport and trade; choices and organization also mattered.

exit_ticket.prompt: HE1. A city has a river but never builds boats or trading places. Does the river guarantee a busy trade network? Explain using the lesson.
exit_ticket.answer: No; access is an opportunity but people must use it. A river alone does not guarantee organized trade.

materials: History video: Ancient Rome 101 by National Geographic. https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/ancient-rome-101/
lessons.voice_prompt: Use the geography/action/result picture. Avoid saying geography made Rome fail. Hold Republic content until this explanation is clear. Teach each word before using it. Show the lesson picture first, then draw one different example on the whiteboard. Ask one question at a time. Keep assigned answers protected. At the time limit, mark unfinished work for review and move to the next subject. Today is the revised 10:30 AM to 3:30 PM day. Math and writing are deferred; do not assign them or use spare time for them. Stop this block at 12:45. Help open the linked National Geographic video. After watching, ask for one observed detail and one question. Do not quiz the new kings, Republic, or Empire preview.
lessons.teacher_notes: September 30 history 12/14 = 86%. Q1-4 and exit correct; Q5 missed the multi-cause point. Repair this before advancing. Revised October 1 schedule. Math and writing deferred at parent request; not missing work and not zero grades.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.lesson_title: Check the ScoutLab You Already Built
lessons.previous_learning: Your saved ScoutLab v2 has more players, editable ratings, Compare, team-need choices, and Shortlist. The September 30 emails did not include a test log or live demonstration, so those checks still need evidence.
lessons.course_context: Day 27 follows the September 30 submitted work. Repair the named gap before moving to the next unit.
learning_objectives: Explain a best-fit choice with the numbers shown
lessons.why_it_matters: Making a page is the start. Checking it helps you trust what it says.

vocabulary.definition: a number used to compare a skill
what you think will happen before you test
the players you save to consider later
two or more players have the same top number
a check of what happens when you use a feature

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 1:15 to 2:10, 55 minutes. Stop and move on at 2:10.
Laptop only. Write your test log in a document on your laptop; do not answer Builder questions on paper. Continue your existing ScoutLab; do not restart or add players. Record all Builder responses on your laptop.
The ratings are practice numbers for this build, not verified real-world facts about the players. A best-fit choice depends on the ratings and the team need you chose.
First select three different players. Write their names so someone else can repeat your check.
Before every test, write your prediction. Then change only what the test asks, click the button, and write what actually happened. A result is evidence when another person can see or repeat it.
TEST A: Give your first player pace 99 and the other two pace 60 and 70. Press Compare. Write who should lead pace before you press it, then record who actually leads.
TEST B: Give the first two players passing 88 and the third 70. Press Compare. A tie means the two highest numbers are equal; both should be listed.
TEST C: Shortlist Player 2. Edit another rating and press Compare. Check that Player 2 is still visibly shortlisted. Check this while the same browser tab stays open. You do not need to close the browser.
TEST D: Keep the same three players and ratings. Switch Need Speed to Need Defense. Explain that a new team need can change best fit because a different skill matters more. The winner does not HAVE to change if one player still fits both needs best.
If a check fails, say: I clicked ___; I expected ___; I saw ___. Ask the coding AI for one focused fix, then repeat the same check. Keep a screenshot of a result and write your own explanation.

worked_examples.title: Describe a visible problem
worked_examples.problem: A Compare page shows Alex leading passing 70 even though Bea has passing 85.
worked_examples.solution: I pressed Compare. Bea should lead passing with 85, but the page shows Alex with 70. Please fix the passing leader and keep the other features working.
worked_examples.explanation: Names, numbers, and the click make the problem easy to repeat.

worked_examples.title: Record a successful check
worked_examples.problem: In an invented practice app, Alex and Bea have catching ratings of 82. Cam has 71. The page lists Alex and Bea together.
worked_examples.solution: Prediction: Alex and Bea should tie. Result: both names appear with 82. Check: worked.
worked_examples.explanation: A useful record includes the names, numbers, and actual result. This is a different skill and set of numbers from your assigned ScoutLab tests.

independent_practice.prompt: B1. Record the names of your three players. For Tests A, B, C, and D, write a prediction, what actually happened, and worked or needs a fix.
independent_practice.answer: Four genuine observed results. Test A first player pace99 leads; B first two tie passing88; C shortlist survives edits/Compare; D explanation of changed priorities even if winner unchanged.

independent_practice.prompt: B2. Save one screenshot showing a comparison result. Label the player names and the feature you checked.
B3. If any check fails, write one fix request, make the change with your coding AI, and repeat that check. If every check works, explain one design choice instead.
independent_practice.answer: Evidence of fix and retest or a clear design explanation.

exit_ticket.prompt: BE1. Show your parent one changed rating, a Compare result, and a saved shortlisted player. Explain why one player fits your chosen team need.
exit_ticket.answer: A witnessed demo or short recording; keep incomplete until observed. Rubric: four logs 8, screenshot2, demo3, explanation2, total15.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: Turn a Vague Clue Into Exact Evidence
lessons.previous_learning: You logged 10 pages and chose Otis Amber. Acting strange did not tell the reader exactly what he did or said. Today you will find one detail that a reader can check.
lessons.course_context: Day 27 follows the September 30 submitted work. Repair the named gap before moving to the next unit.
learning_objectives: Give a detail a reader can find
Separate a book fact from your idea
Explain why you kept or changed a theory
lessons.why_it_matters: A mystery theory becomes stronger when you can show the clue behind it.

vocabulary.definition: one specific thing someone does or says
a detail that might help solve the mystery
an idea that may change with more evidence
an idea you draw from a detail
another possible explanation

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 2:20 to 3:10, 50 minutes. Stop and move on at 3:10.
Keep reading The Westing Game from your bookmark. First spend up to 5 minutes finding the page you used for yesterday's Otis Amber idea. Write the page or chapter and the exact action or words. If you cannot find it, choose a different detail you can point to and say you changed the clue.
Read independently for 25 minutes. Virgil stays quiet unless you ask for a word meaning. Write the starting page and ending page using your own edition.
After reading, use the picture: detail, where I found it, my idea, another possibility, keep or change my idea.
MODEL FROM A DIFFERENT STORY: At page 12, Kai hides a wet umbrella behind the door. I think he may have been outside. Another possibility is that he borrowed someone else's wet umbrella. The wet umbrella supports my first idea but does not prove it.
Acting strange is too vague. Instead say exactly what the character did or said and where you found it. Your theory can be uncertain; your detail must be clear.
Do not look up suspects or later chapters. Keep every idea within the pages you have read. The Westing Game's 8 homeschool reading points remain pending until you finish and pass the comprehension check.

worked_examples.title: Detail and inference are different
worked_examples.problem: Kai hides a wet umbrella behind the door in an invented mystery.
worked_examples.solution: Detail: he hides a wet umbrella. Idea: he may have been outside. Another possibility: he borrowed it.
worked_examples.explanation: The detail is visible in the story; the explanation is your idea, so use may or might.

worked_examples.title: Change an idea when a new detail appears
worked_examples.problem: In an invented mystery, Kai hides a wet umbrella. Later, he says he borrowed it from his sister.
worked_examples.solution: I change my idea that Kai was outside. The umbrella may have been wet before he borrowed it.
worked_examples.explanation: An exact new detail can change the meaning of an earlier clue. This invented example does not describe The Westing Game.

independent_practice.prompt: L1. Repair yesterday's clue. Name the character, exact action or words, and page or chapter. If you replace the clue, say so.
independent_practice.answer: Specific verifiable detail from pages actually read; no unsupported book fact awarded.

independent_practice.prompt: L2. Record today's starting and ending page. Read for 25 minutes from your bookmark.
independent_practice.answer: Actual page range and reading time recorded; no forced chapter jump.

independent_practice.prompt: L3. Choose one exact detail from today's reading. Write where you found it, what you think it means, and one other possible meaning.
independent_practice.answer: Detail plus location, evidence-linked inference, plausible alternative.

independent_practice.prompt: L4. Write one question about the detail and a one-sentence theory.
independent_practice.answer: Question and theory tied to the chosen detail.

exit_ticket.prompt: LE1. Circle keep or change for your earlier theory. Explain how today's exact detail affects it.
exit_ticket.answer: An explicit decision with a reason tied to the exact detail, no spoilers. Rubric exact detail/location3, inference2, alternative2, question1, change/keep and reason2; total10.

lessons.voice_prompt: No spoilers and no invented Westing Game events. Ask Atticus to show the page before checking a detail. Stay quiet during independent reading. Use only the invented umbrella example for modelling. Teach each word before using it. Show the lesson picture first, then draw one different example on the whiteboard. Ask one question at a time. Keep assigned answers protected. At the time limit, mark unfinished work for review and move to the next subject. Today is the revised 10:30 AM to 3:30 PM day. Math and writing are deferred; do not assign them or use spare time for them. Stop this block at 3:10.
